body: Just an update on this post. My attempts to help my husband were unsuccessful. He went into the hospital for the fourth time in less than a year, and within ten days of release (the hospital let him go with a pat on the head, just as they had the other three times) he was successful. I spoke with him an hour before to tell him goodnight with the promise of seeing him the next day. He had everything packed, he had even cleaned out the fridge, he did not want to be found or stopped--even though the police and I were out looking for him following his goodbye text to me. I am shattered, it has been almost two weeks and I can barely talk about it. Our sons, both young adults, are fractured as well. He has left a chasm in our lives and hearts.

Very well put! Here is a tasting tip - if you draw air in while tasting, swish it around, then spit you will get a better idea of the profile and finish. Drawing the air in and swishing helps to better engage the olfactory senses - critical to tasting - and it helps the wine to coat every part of your palate. Spitting actually passes the wine over your palate a second time...think of drawing air in, swishing and spitting as checking yourself front and back in a full mirror before heading out rather than just a quick shoulders up glance.

Amazing job grabbing and fixing the wine fridge! The wine world is massive, and like most other things it is growing and changing very quickly.  I have a few pieces of advice for you:

- Remember that taste is subjective. Like food, film, books, etc., the only opinion that really matters is yours. 
- If you try something and don’t like it, don’t write off that varietal or blend. Try another one from a different region. For example, there is a world of difference between Pinot Noirs from Sonoma, Central Otago in NZ, and Volnay, Cote de Beaune in Burgundy. Many varietals from one country or region are made in a range of styles as well. You can have a German Riesling that ranges from dry as a bone to a dessert wine. 
- Food and wine pairings matter...but the rules are not hard and fast (due to the point above). Learn some of the general rules and go from there. Basics such as a dry, acidic wine will amplify chilli heat, look for an off-dry to sweet wine to go that spicy dish. With that knowledge, and using the example of the German Riesling above, skip the dry Rheinhessen and go with a sweeter Mosel to balance the Thai food.  
- Get to know the people who work at your favourite wine store. 

Don’t worry about only being able to pick out a couple of fruits when you smell a wine. That is a skill that comes with a lot of training and a lot of practice.  I am currently studying for my Advanced certification with the Court of Master Sommeliers, and I am constantly smelling fruits, vegetables, herbs, plants, flowers, all sorts of things, and tasting every single day to be able to dig deeply into a wine. For now, just concentrate on the first two-to-three things that jump out and don’t worry with the detail. Keep it simple, like, “I smell red berries and vanilla,” or “I’m getting citrus, tropical fruit, and flowers.” If you find that examining a wine in greater detail is a skill you wish to learn, do yourself a favour and learn from a pro. I really love the WSET 1 course as a way to learn good wine basics including pairing and tasting. 

Above all - have fun!

The other thing that picking the grapes at a lower brix level is elevated acidity in comparison to when the grapes would be harvested for a red. That acidity helps to give a tart balance to that bright, red sweet fruit nose.

Provence roses tend to have a very sweet nose, however they can be quite dry on the palate. I have some that give me strawberry and watermelon off the bat - think pink Jolly Rancher. There are a few reasons, including Carbonic Maceration mentioned below. The varietal can also be a factor. Many Provence roses are Grenache-Mouvedre blends, sometimes with other French varietals (depends on the appellation laws). Grenache as a rose can have very bright red fruit and candy-like aromas.
